about.title: Livingston Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Livingston's economy runs on agriculture, food processing, and the trucking that moves goods along Walnut Avenue and Main Street, and jobs in those industries carry real physical risk. When a worker gets hurt, California's workers' compensation system usually pays medical bills and a portion of lost wages regardless of who caused the accident, but that system doesn't allow a lawsuit against your employer in most cases. What it doesn't cover is a separate claim against a negligent third party, like a subcontractor, an equipment manufacturer, a delivery driver, or a property owner whose carelessness contributed to your injury. Livingston workers, whether they're in a cold storage warehouse, on a dairy operation, or driving a route through town, may have both a workers' comp claim and a third-party claim running at the same time. LawProactive doesn't practice law; we simply connect injured workers with an independent attorney, free of charge, who can look at the specifics of your job and your accident and explain what options actually apply to you.

whyChoose.title: Why Livingston Workers Reach Out to LawProactive

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Story
items.desc: Workers' compensation is usually your only remedy against your employer, but if a third party like a subcontractor, equipment maker, or another driver contributed to your injury, a separate claim may be possible.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Matter
items.desc: California generally requires you to report a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days, and missing that window can complicate your claim, so getting guidance early helps protect your options.

items.title: Retaliation Is Illegal, and You Have Recourse
items.desc: An employer cannot legally punish or fire you for reporting an injury or filing a workers' comp claim, and an independent attorney can help you understand your rights if that happens.

items.question: I work at a food processing plant in Livingston. Can I still file a workers' comp claim if the accident was partly my fault?
items.answer: Yes, California workers' compensation generally doesn't require you to prove fault; it's designed to cover work injuries regardless of who caused them. The tradeoff is that it usually prevents you from suing your employer directly. If a third party outside your employer contributed to the accident, that's a separate matter worth having an attorney review.

items.question: What if my injury happened on a delivery route near Main Street or Hammatt Avenue, not at my regular job site?
items.answer: An injury that happens while you're performing work duties, even away from your usual location, is typically still covered by workers' compensation. If another driver or a third party caused the crash, you may also have a separate injury claim against them, and the driving-injury data in this area shows collisions do happen along those corridors. An independent attorney can sort out which claims apply.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a claim if a third party caused my work injury in Merced County?
items.answer: Third-party injury claims in California generally carry a two-year deadline from the date of the injury. Workers' comp reporting has its own separate 30-day window with your employer. Because these timelines run differently, it's worth getting a free consultation sooner rather than later so nothing gets missed.
